theme: Every Warrior Blows Their Own Conch
hindi: हृषीकेश श्रीकृष्ण ने पाञ्चजन्य नामक शंख बजाया और धनंजय अर्जुन ने देवदत्त नामक शंख बजाया। भयंकर कर्म करने वाले, भोजन-प्रिय भीम ने अपना विशाल शंख पौण्ड्र बजाया।
english: Krishna, the master of the senses, blew his conch Panchajanya, and Arjuna, the winner of wealth, blew his conch Devadatta. Bhima, the wolf-bellied doer of mighty deeds, blew his great conch Paundra.
deeper: This verse is like a roll call of sounds. After Bhishma’s lion-roar and the great noise of drums and horns, the Pandava side answers one by one. Each hero has his own named conch: Krishna’s Panchajanya, Arjuna’s Devadatta (meaning “god-given”), and Bhima’s Paundra. Each had a different sound, and each was blown with full confidence.

The names also tell us about the people. Krishna is called Hrishikesha, “master of the senses”. He is calm and in control even in the middle of a battlefield. Arjuna is Dhananjaya, “winner of wealth”. Bhima is Vrikodara, “wolf-belly”, because of his great hunger and strength, and Bhima-karma, because his deeds were mighty. Every person on a team brings a different gift.

There is a quiet lesson here too. A conch is only a shell until someone breathes into it. In the same way, our talents become useful only when we put effort and courage behind them. The conches also remind us that a team is made of many voices, but they are all working for one purpose.
words: the conch named Panchajanya, Krishna’s conch
Krishna, the lord and master of the senses
the one whose deeds are mighty and fearsome
Bhima, the “wolf-bellied” one, known for his great appetite and strength
background: The two great armies stood ready at Kurukshetra. To cheer Duryodhana, the elder Bhishma roared like a lion and blew his conch (1.12). Then conches, drums and horns blared together in one tremendous roar (1.13).

Next, Krishna and Arjuna, seated in their grand chariot drawn by white horses, blew their divine conches (1.14). Verse 1.15 now names the conches of Krishna, Arjuna and Bhima, so we hear the Pandava side answer back one by one.
lessons: Each person has a special talent or voice, and the team needs all of them.
Krishna stays steady even in a noisy, scary place, and we can learn to stay calm too.
Bhima’s strength was famous because he used it to help and defend others.
A conch makes no sound until someone blows into it, just as our gifts grow when we practise.
The Pandavas replied to the challenge boldly instead of hiding, and courage means facing what comes.
examples: In Meera’s school band, Ravi plays the drum, Anita plays the flute and Meera sings. The music sounds beautiful because each one plays their own part.
Karan is a fast bowler, Imran is a good fielder and Sneha hits big sixes. They win because every player does what they do best.
At Diwali, Aarav’s family makes sweets together. One person stirs, one rolls and one decorates. Everyone’s job matters.
Before her class play, Divya feels nervous. She takes a slow breath like Krishna, who stays calm in a noisy place, and then walks on stage.
Four friends make a chart about the solar system. One draws, one writes, one colours and one speaks. Each brings a different strength.
Bhavesh is the tallest and strongest boy in class. He helps a smaller friend carry heavy books instead of showing off.
Tara wants to blow the conch at the puja, but at first no sound comes. She practises every evening and soon the sound rings out.
Nikhil is shy, but he has a good idea for the class fair. He takes a deep breath and shares it, and his friends love it.

story.title: Bhima and the Hungry Demon
paras: When the Pandavas were hiding in the village of Ekachakra, they stayed in the house of a kind Brahmin family. One day Kunti found the family crying. A demon named Baka lived near the village. Each week one family had to send him a cartload of food, along with the person who drove it, and Baka would eat both.
That week it was this family’s turn. Kunti could not bear their sorrow. She said, “My son Bhima will take the food.” The family was shocked, but Kunti trusted her strong, big-hearted son.

Bhima drove the cart to the forest. Then, as the story goes, he began eating the food himself and calling out to Baka. The angry demon rushed at him, and they fought fiercely. In the end, Bhima defeated Baka and dragged him back, and the people of Ekachakra were free from fear.
Bhima’s strength was never just for showing off. He used it to protect people who were afraid. That is why, in the Gita, he is remembered as the doer of mighty deeds, Bhima-karma.
story.moral: Lesson: Real strength is best used to protect others, and every person’s gift has its own special place in the team.

quiz.x: Hrishikesha, which is Krishna, blew Panchajanya.

quiz.q: What does the name Devadatta, Arjuna’s conch, mean?

o: He had a wolf-like belly and huge appetite
quiz.x: Vrikodara means “wolf-bellied”, a name for Bhima’s great hunger and strength.

quiz.q: What is the main lesson of this verse for us?
o: Everyone has a special voice and gift to add to the team
quiz.x: Each hero blew his own conch, showing that every person’s gift matters.

reel.hook: Even a conch makes no sound until someone blows. What about you?
reel.lesson: Everyone has a special gift, so add your own voice to the team.
reel.caption:
Krishna, Arjuna and Bhima each blew their own conch, and each one mattered 🐚
What is your special gift today?
Share it with your team 💛
